newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel spent $2.7 bln to aid exchange rate.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel spent $2.7 bln to aid exchange rate.

text.p: The Bank of Israel bought $2.7 billion in foreign currency in the first two months of the year in a bid to support the currency basket rate against the shekel, the daily newspaper Haaretz reported on Thursday.
As a result, said Haaretz, citing an internal Bank of Israel document, the central bank injected 8.9 billion shekels into the economy.

A Bank of Israel spokesman told Reuters the bank had successfully absorbed all of the shekels flowing into the economy by its intervention in the local currency market and did not regard it as a monetary injection at all.
"After you clean it up in the capital market, the injection is nil," the spokesman said.

Israel's money supply rose a sharp 3.4 percent in January, and economists said today they expected the central bank to report another 2.5 percent to three percent rise for February. But the Bank of Israel spokesman said there was no connection with the bank's intervention in the forex market.
He attributed the rise mainly to lower interest rates -- the Bank of Israel has lowered the base rate 3.1 percent since August 1996 -- and to expectations of lower inflation.
In the first two months of this year, the Treasury absorbed 900 million shekels, because it raised more money in the domestic capital market than it required to cover overspending, Haaretz said.

The central bank has been regularly intervening in the local foreign currency market in a bid to keep the currency basket rate, to which the Israeli shekel is officially pegged, from falling below its trading band. The band allows the shekel to move seven percent above or below a sliding midpoint.
